1.explanation:
• components/prism-apex.js & .min.js: These files define Prism.languages.apex = Prism.languages.java. Without them, Prism has no ‘apex’ grammar.
• components/index.js: This file exports all language definitions. We must import and register prism-apex.js here so it’s included in the bundle.
• plugins/autoloader/prism-autoloader.js: The autoloader maps file extensions to language IDs. We must add {"apex":"apex"} so that loading .cls or .trigger files will fetch the new apex component.
• components.js: This generated manifest lists all available components for the custom build builder. Adding ‘apex’ here makes it show up in the languages list.
• gulpfile.js/paths.js: The build scripts use this file to know which source files to process, watch, and include in the output. We need to add prism-apex.js (and its .min.js) to the components paths so that it’s copied into the final distribution.
1.bug_scenario: The user is trying to highlight Salesforce’s Apex code in Prism and has aliased it to Java, but Prism does not ship with an “apex” language definition. In the screenshot you can see an “Apex” label in the UI but no syntax highlighting rules apply, because Prism only knows “java.” To add support we need to create an apex definition that simply points at Prism.languages.java and wire it into the build and loader.

2.bug_scenario: The user wants Prism to recognize “Apex” as a first-class language in addition to Java. In the screenshot they’ve tagged the code block with “Apex” but it still highlights as plain text because there is no Prism component for Apex. The proposal is to alias Prism.languages.apex to Prism.languages.java so that Apex syntax will be colored exactly as Java. Currently there is no prism-apex.js (or its minified equivalent) in the components folder, nor is “apex” registered in the components index or build configuration.
